query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, elevated-temperature degradation in oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by the combined effects of (i) short-circuit diffusion along AM cellular/subgrain boundaries and high dislocation density, and (ii) element partitioning that sequesters Al and Ti into L12-type Ni3(Ti,Al) precipitates. This combination lowers the effective Al/Ti activity in the fcc matrix and accelerates outward Cr transport, favoring formation of non-protective (Ni,Co)Cr2O4 spinel plus TiO2 and internal oxidation of Al/Ti along short-circuit paths. The near-surface depletion of Al/Ti undermines precipitation strengthening and fatigue resistance. In reducing gases (e.g., dry H2), external oxide formation is suppressed but hydrogen ingress along short-circuit paths promotes vacancy clustering and precipitate coarsening/dissolution near the surface, producing similar loss of near-surface strength/fatigue integrity without changing the bulk fcc matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy, single-phase fcc matrix designed for formability, with as-built AM cellular/subgrain structure and high dislocation density; potential fine L12 Ni3(Ti,Al) nanoprecipitates contributing to noted strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Thermal exposure at elevated temperature to oxidizing gas (e.g., air) or reducing gas (e.g., dry H2), with controlled microstructural preparation to vary short-circuit diffusion and Al/Ti partitioning (solutionized vs aged vs as-built).
generation.conditions: Temperatures in the range 700–900 °C; oxidizing exposure at pO2 ~0.21 atm (air) or controlled pO2 > 10^-4 atm; reducing exposure in dry H2 with very low pH2O (pO2 < 10^-20 atm). Exposure durations up to 100 h.
generation.structural_mediator: AM-induced cellular/subgrain boundary network and dislocation density acting as short-circuit diffusion pathways; L12 Ni3(Ti,Al) precipitates (volume fraction and distribution) that sequester Al/Ti and lower their activity in the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Lower Al/Ti activity in the fcc matrix due to precipitation and segregation, together with fast short-circuit diffusion, leads to preferential outward diffusion of Cr and formation of (Ni,Co)Cr2O4 spinel and TiO2 at the surface rather than continuous Al2O3. Oxygen penetrates along cellular boundaries causing internal oxidation of Al/Ti and formation of discrete oxides beneath the surface, generating a near-surface depletion zone of Al/Ti and reduced L12 strengthening. Under reducing gases, hydrogen ingress along the same short-circuit paths enhances vacancy concentrations and promotes precipitate coarsening/dissolution near the surface, causing softening and increased fatigue crack propagation, while the bulk fcc matrix remains intact.
generation.predicted_outcome:
- Oxidizing gas (air): relative to the starting-state baseline, higher oxidation rate and mass gain than expected for a protective chromia/alumina former; surface scale dominated by (Ni,Co)Cr2O4 spinel with TiO2 islands; measurable internal oxidation of Al/Ti along cellular boundaries (depth on the order of several to tens of micrometers, magnitude uncertain); near-surface depletion of Al/Ti and reduced L12 precipitate fraction, producing a measurable decrease in near-surface hardness and degraded fatigue crack growth resistance.
- Reducing gas (dry H2): minimal net mass change; increased hydrogen content near the surface; observable coarsening or reduction of L12 precipitates within a near-surface zone and associated softening; increased fatigue crack growth rate or reduced fatigue life relative to the baseline, with the bulk fcc matrix unchanged.
generation.baseline: As-built AM alloy prior to exposure: single-phase fcc matrix with noted strength and fatigue resistance; no surface oxide scale, intact L12-strengthening contribution (if present), and uniform near-surface hardness.
generation.boundary: Predictions apply when Al content/activity is subcritical for continuous Al2O3 formation (as in the given composition) and when short-circuit diffusion paths are present. If the microstructure is fully recrystallized and homogenized to remove cellular boundaries and if Al/Ti remain in solid solution at sufficient activity, behavior may shift. At very low temperatures (<600 °C) diffusion-limited processes may be too slow; at very high temperatures (>1000 °C) phase stability changes could alter oxide selection and invalidate predictions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact oxidation kinetics (mass gain rate), internal oxidation depth, and quantitative changes in precipitate volume fraction and mechanical property degradation are uncertain without direct measurement. The presence and stability of L12 Ni3(Ti,Al) precipitates in the starting alloy and their response to hydrogen at the specified temperatures require confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three microstructural states of the same composition: (A) as-built AM, (B) solutionized/homogenized and recrystallized to minimize cellular boundaries and dissolve precipitates (e.g., high-temperature solution treatment followed by rapid quench), and (C) aged to enhance L12 Ni3(Ti,Al) precipitation. Expose samples to air at 800 °C for 100 h and to dry H2 at 800 °C for 100 h. Use matched coupons and identical surface finish. Assess oxidation kinetics and near-surface microstructural/property changes.
measurements: Thermogravimetric mass gain vs time during oxidizing exposure
Surface and cross-sectional oxide phase identification (XRD, Raman) and morphology (SEM)
Elemental maps and profiles (EDS/EPMA) for Al, Ti, Cr, Ni, Co to quantify depletion and internal oxidation depth
Transmission electron microscopy near-surface to quantify L12 precipitate fraction/size before and after exposure
Hydrogen content via thermal desorption spectroscopy after reducing exposure
Fatigue crack growth rate (da/dN–ΔK) before and after exposures for each state
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) Removing short-circuit diffusion paths and dissolving precipitates (state B) does not reduce oxidation rate, internal oxidation depth, or change the oxide from spinel/TiO2 toward a more protective scale compared to as-built (state A); (2) Increasing L12 precipitation (state C) does not increase spinel-dominant oxidation and Al/Ti depletion near the surface relative to state B; or (3) Reducing gas exposure does not increase near-surface hydrogen content, does not alter precipitate stability, and does not measurably degrade near-surface hardness or fatigue behavior compared to baseline.
